passage: Ms Nair's class was doing fractions on the board. Pooja wasn't sure of the answer, but her hand went up anyway. “Three-sixths?” she said. “Not quite,” said the teacher, smiling, “but let's see how you got there.” Pooja explained, and the teacher wrote her steps on the board. “Look, Pooja found half the puzzle. Who can find the rest?” A boy giggled at the back. “We all learn by being wrong,” the teacher said mildly, and the giggle stopped. Abhinav, who never spoke in class, kept his hand low, though his eyes followed the chalk. Three more hands went up.

qa.q: What fraction did Pooja offer as her answer?
Why did Pooja raise her hand even though she was not sure of the answer?
qa.a: Pooja seems to feel safe being wrong in this room, because mistakes here are treated as part of learning. 🙂

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped children keep volunteering?
qa.a: The teacher asked how Pooja got there, wrote her steps on the board, and stopped the giggle mildly while calling wrong answers a way to learn.

qa.q: What might Abhinav be thinking as his eyes follow the chalk while his hand stays low?
qa.a: Abhinav may be interested and slowly gaining trust that a wrong answer will be safe, but is not ready yet to speak.

grounding: A child in a warm classroom raises a hand though unsure because mistakes are treated as part of learning.

passage: I'm Harsha, and I sit two rows behind Harish. Harish hadn't put a hand up all term. Today the teacher asked what one-half plus one-quarter was, and Harish's hand went up slowly. “Two-sixths?” he said. I held my breath. Nobody laughed. The teacher wrote it on the board and said, “That's a very useful mistake. It shows us what happens when we add the bottoms.” Harish's ears turned red. I can't tell what he felt. But when the next question came, his hand went up again, a bit faster.

qa.q: Where does Harsha sit compared with Harish?
qa.a: Harsha sits two rows behind Harish.

qa.q: What might Harish have been feeling when Harish's ears turned red?
qa.a: Harish may have felt exposed and shy after speaking, though Harsha can't be sure. The hand going up faster for the next question suggests the moment felt safe enough.

qa.q: What could the teacher do next to keep Harish volunteering?
qa.a: The teacher could keep treating mistakes as useful, call on Harish when a hand goes up and praise the effort, not just the right answer.

qa.q: How might Harsha have felt watching Harish's hand go up again?
qa.a: Harsha, who had held a breath in case anyone laughed, probably felt relieved and glad for Harish when the hand rose faster the second time.

grounding: An observer watches a child who never volunteered answer unsure in a class where mistakes are treated as part of learning.
